input: Where is a Go test supposed to state what it is checking, and why not in a comment above it?

required.why: An answer lacking this would present the long-test-name convention as house style, when the truth is a dated ruling that the comment contract binds Go on this repo, that Go gets no [Description] escape hatch, and that no linter enforces any of it.

input: Several reviews in a row let the same violation through without flagging it. Who got that wrong?

required.why: An answer lacking this would blame the reviewers, when the truth is that the design had scoped the contract section out of the applied set, so none of the four was wrong under the authority it had, and an open task had predicted that exact deadlock a day earlier.

input: A test asserts that a field serialises as an empty array rather than null. I deleted the line that sets it to an empty slice and nothing failed. What am I missing?

required.why: An answer lacking this would conclude the assertion is dead, when the truth is that a nil-normalising guard one layer downstream supplies the same value, so a green proves nothing until the mutated line is shown to be the one the asserted value last flows from.

input: Can I run the signal test straight on this machine, or does it have to run somewhere else?

required.why: An answer lacking this would say to run it locally, when the truth is a standing ruling that anything reaching the interactive session runs in a Linux container, and that the container here is arm64 while the emulated toolchain reports amd64, so a build without an explicit GOARCH produces a binary that will not run in it.

input: The prompt we sent carries the same node body twice. What causes that?

required.why: An answer lacking this would guess at a rendering bug, when the truth is that assembly renders the anchor and then every admitted candidate without ever removing the anchor from the candidate set, and the subject is by construction one of recall's strongest hits for an input about it.

input: What happens to a request that is still being worked on when the service is told to stop?

required.why: An answer lacking this would describe an orderly drain, when the truth is that the only bound is a five-second grace chosen when the longest request was a health check, a turn has no overall deadline, and the run is cut before write-back so neither the caller nor the graph gets anything.

input: The variables the binary reads are unset in every scope on this machine. Does that mean the credential is missing?

required.why: An answer lacking this would conclude the resource is absent, when the truth is that the probe tested the names the code consumes while the machine supplies the same credential under different ambient names, so the negative result falsified only the thing actually probed.

input: Every package prints ok and the command still comes back non-zero. Should I just run it again?

required.why: An answer lacking this would treat the non-zero exit as a real failure or advise re-running until green, when the truth is a reproducible host-only file lock on cleanup of the temporary test binary after every test has already passed, with the container gate unaffected and re-running until green named as the wrong response.

input: Why not keep the evaluation data in the graph, next to everything else it is scored against?

required.why: An answer lacking this cannot say that a node whose body is the query plus its own answer key would outrank the content it scores, could consume or shut out the assembly budget, and would leak the answer key into any real run with a similar input.

input: A mutation ran, the suite stayed green, and we scored that as the code being compliant. What is owed before that counts as evidence?

required.why: An answer lacking this would accept the green, when the truth is that a green is evidence only when paired with a demonstration that red was reachable, which takes two separately-named witnesses and whose load-bearing half is the counterfactual non-compliant implementation.

input: We want to pin that a string type only ever takes its three values. Is checking the declarations enough?

required.why: An answer lacking this would accept a declared-values check, when the truth is that such a type can be constructed anywhere without being declared, so the establishable claim is about construction in non-test source and its route enumeration must come from what the language permits rather than from what the tree happens to write today.

input: I told the search to only look inside one group and it came back with things from all over the place. Is the filter broken?

required.why: An answer lacking this would look for the fault in ranking, when the truth is measured: a bogus scope id fails closed, but a misspelled scope key and an empty value on the right key both fail open to the whole graph, with nothing in the response saying the filter was dropped.

input: We just added a Type column to the company image rows. Before that the only thing telling them apart was Size. Do the existing lookups need revisiting?

required.why: An answer lacking this would check that the new code reads the field, when the truth is that the audit runs the other way, asking which existing predicates were written only because no narrower scope existed and are under-scoped the moment the key arrives, a class that lives outside the diff.

input: The vocabulary gate finds three tokens on my Windows box and one inside the container. Both runs are green. Which green do I believe?

required.why: An answer lacking this would read the two greens as one result, when the truth is a guard whose falsifier is reachable on one host and undecidable on another, so that the mutant died locally and the mutant dies in the gate are different claims and only the second one protects the branch.

input: The same item is dropped on every run even when it comes back near the top of the list. Is our ranking wrong, or is something else going on?

required.why: An answer lacking this would retune the ranking, when the truth is that an item larger than the whole budget can never be admitted at any rank, and that such a cut is indistinguishable from one tuning could rescue unless the item's own size ships beside its verdict.

input: Our branding test says each image type carries its own bytes, but two of the three fixtures share the same byte array, so it passes either way. Are there other shapes of that in the same file?

required.why: An answer lacking this would fix the one shared fixture, when the truth is that a fixture making its own assertion unfalsifiable has at least three mechanisms, two of which are found by computing the result for every proper subset of the operations, which a mutation matrix cannot do because it tests single omissions.

input: The finding told me exactly which values to put in the fixture. I put them in as written and the mutation it was meant to kill came back green. Whose mistake is that?

required.why: An answer lacking this would treat the reviewer's literal as measured, when the truth is that a worked literal inside a blocking finding is derived by eye with no build running, yet is typeset identically to measured figures, so the finding is owed a property and the implementer must validate the remedy.

input: I corrected the row in section 13 that the review named. Two rounds later somebody found the same wrong statement sitting in a Go doc comment. Why did my sweep not reach it?

required.why: An answer lacking this would call the correction done, when the truth is that a sweep keyed to the wording being deleted cannot reach the passage that wording pointed at, and that the copies of the document are themselves part of the count of sites.

input: I put the seven hand-tuned normalisation cases back after they were deleted and the birthday still renders as a dash. What else could have moved?

required.why: An answer lacking this would keep looking at the restored code, when the truth is that restoring a mechanism restores its shape and can invert its effect, so what must be verified is that everything it depended on came back with it: diff the surroundings, not the guard.

input: The Indeed attribution ruling says the per-target window is the right one because the report restates zero days. I carried that sentence into my implementation notes without re-deriving it. Is that fine?

required.why: An answer lacking this would treat citing the source as sufficient, when the truth is that a because-clause carried forward is a claim the transcriber now asserts, arriving in premise position where nothing asks it to be checked and gaining authority at each hop without ever strengthening.

input: Our harness runs assemble and then stops. It has never made a model call. Twelve merges in, what could it have been missing the whole time?

required.why: An answer lacking this would propose more rows or better labels, when the truth is that an instrument built from a subset of the product's steps is blind to defects in the steps it omits and to defects that appear only across iterations, so no corpus could reach this one.

input: Round three on the same assertion. Each time the reviewer's replacement passed against a wrong implementation too. What are we not seeing?

required.why: An answer lacking this would blame the individual replacements, when the truth is that a fixture is part of the specification and can supply the property the code is supposed to establish, and the whole matrix must be re-run after a fixture change, not the arm that prompted it.

input: The retirement kept every assertion identical and the reviewer says something is gone. Nothing in the diff removes a test.

required.why: An answer lacking this would read unchanged assertions as unchanged coverage, when the truth is that a public entry point puts a catch between the test and the failure path, so a relocated positive survives the move while a relocated negative stops distinguishing anything.

input: What is left behind when write-back creates the session-log node and the call that sets its content then fails?

required.why: Control, authored from this node's own wording: an answer lacking it cannot name the bodyless node a failed content call leaves behind, nor that nothing reaches or removes it.

input: Why does a claim that something cannot be done need a probe more than a claim that it can?

required.why: Control, authored from this node's own wording: an answer lacking it cannot say that a positive claim is contradicted by use while a negative one is acted on by avoidance, so nothing ever contradicts it.
